1.pericope_label: And it came to pass after this, that David enquired of the Lord, saying, Shall I go up into any of the cities of Judah? And the Lord said unto him, Go up. And David said, Whither shall I go up? And he said, Unto Hebron. So David went up thither, and his two wives also, Ahinoam the Jezreelitess, and Abigail Nabal’s wife the Carmelite. And his men that were with him did David bring up, every man with his household: and they dwelt in the cities of Hebron. And the men of Judah came, and there they anointed David king over the house of Judah. And they told David, saying, That the men of Jabesh–gilead were they that buried Saul. And David sent messengers unto the men of Jabesh–gilead, and said unto them, Blessed be ye of the Lord, that ye have shewed this kindness unto your lord, even unto Saul, and have buried him. And now the Lord shew kindness and truth unto you: and I also will requite you this kindness, because ye have done this thing. Therefore now let your hands be strengthened, and be ye valiant: for your master Saul is dead, and also the house of Judah have anointed me king over them.

schools.summary: Henry makes the pace of the accession the lesson, since David knew himself anointed and saw his way clear yet sent no messengers summoning allegiance on pain of death but proceeded leisurely, he that believeth not making haste; and though the force gathered at Ziklag might have brought him in by conquest, he that will rule with meekness will not rise with violence. He draws the rule that assurance of hope in a promise quickens endeavour rather than slackening it, calls Hebron a priest's city and a city of refuge where God made himself a little sanctuary, notes that the patriarchs' sepulchres adjoining would recall the ancient promise and that David was not sent to Bethlehem because it was little among the thousands of Judah, observes that Judah had often stood by itself and now anointed him over its own house only, reads the gradual rise as a figure of the Son of David, and breaks the Jabesh embassy into four acts, the commendation, the prayer, the promise to requite and the prudent turn to gain them, remarking of the third that good wishes are good things but too cheap where there is ability to do more.

Clarke distinguishes the two anointings by their legal effect, the earlier giving a right to the kingdom and this one authority over it, calls the embassy to Jabesh-gilead highly indicative of the grandeur of David's mind since Saul had greatly injured him and was still reverenced as the anointed of God, reaches for Saurin, who told Louis the formidable prince that he had once honoured him as his king and still reverenced him as the scourge of the Lord, and adds the political motive, that David feared the men of Jabesh would attach themselves to Saul's house in gratitude for the rescue from Nahash. Wesley puts the same legal point without the Latin, that the first anointing only designated the person who should be king and was no actual inauguration, which is why a third was needed when all Israel accepted him; he adds that David asked not whether he should take the kingdom, that being appointed, but only where he should enter upon it, and that Hebron stood in the very centre of the tribe so the whole tribe might speedily resort to it.

Ellicott counts all three anointings and pairs them with Saul's, a private anointing in token of the divine commission, recognition by one tribe, and acceptance by the nation; he supplies the strategy of Hebron, that with most of the land in Philistine hands after the recent defeat a strong town at the far south was peculiarly fitting for a reign to begin in, finds that the Hebrew of the Jabesh message conveys no future recompense but that David as rightful king publicly shows them this good, and notes the old tie between a Benjamite king and the city whose four hundred virgins had been given to the surviving Benjamites. Keil and Delitzsch read the rival promotion as more than Saul's hostility continued, an open act of rebellion against the God who had rejected Saul and chosen David.
Gill dates the enquiry to the day after the fast for Saul and Jonathan.

8.pericope_label: But Abner the son of Ner, captain of Saul’s host, took Ish–bosheth the son of Saul, and brought him over to Mahanaim; And made him king over Gilead, and over the Ashurites, and over Jezreel, and over Ephraim, and over Benjamin, and over all Israel. Ish–bosheth Saul’s son was forty years old when he began to reign over Israel, and reigned two years. But the house of Judah followed David. And the time that David was king in Hebron over the house of Judah was seven years and six months. And Abner the son of Ner, and the servants of Ish–bosheth the son of Saul, went out from Mahanaim to Gibeon. And Joab the son of Zeruiah, and the servants of David, went out, and met together by the pool of Gibeon: and they sat down, the one on the one side of the pool, and the other on the other side of the pool. And Abner said to Joab, Let the young men now arise, and play before us. And Joab said, Let them arise. Then there arose and went over by number twelve of Benjamin, which pertained to Ish–bosheth the son of Saul, and twelve of the servants of David. And they caught every one his fellow by the head, and thrust his sword in his fellow’s side; so they fell down together: wherefore that place was called Helkath–hazzurim, which is in Gibeon. And there was a very sore battle that day; and Abner was beaten, and the men of Israel, before the servants of David.

schools.summary: Henry offers three motives for Abner, zeal for the lineal succession, affection to his own family, or the want of any other way to keep the post of captain of the host, and draws the lesson that one man's pride may occasion great mischief since Ishbosheth would never have set up himself; he sees in the rivalry a type of the Messiah's kingdom, against which the heathen rage and the rulers take counsel. On the chronology he leaves the question open, suggesting Abner declared for the house of Saul in general rather than any one person. On the challenge he takes the proposal as sport in earnest, suspecting Saul had used his men to such barbarous pastimes and Abner had learnt from him to make a jest of wounds and death, holding that fools thus make a mock at sin and that a man is unworthy the name who can throw about firebrands and ask whether he is not in sport; he faults Joab too, who had wisdom enough not to propose it and not resolution enough to refuse it, standing on a point of honour. He renders the place-name the field of rocky men, strong not only in body but of unshaken constancy, and reports from Josephus that the champions despatched one another with mutual wounds as if by agreement.

Keil and Delitzsch reject the older solution of two years over Judah and five and a half over Israel as at variance with the plain statement of the text, read Abner's motive for the single combat as probably a wish to avoid an actual civil war, and note that the combat decided nothing, so a fierce general battle followed in which Abner was put to flight. Ellicott puts four or five years between Saul's death and the coronation, arguing from David's seven and a half years before all Israel acknowledged him, from the Philistine hold on the north, and from Ishbosheth's being the youngest son and now forty; he reads the challenge as Keil and Delitzsch do, to spare bloodshed between tribes of common parentage and keep the nation from weakening before the Philistines, and on Hervey's suggestion compares the Horatii and the Curiatii in Livy, of strikingly similar circumstance and result. On the place-name he reports the margin's field of strong men, judges the etymology doubtful, and says most modern expositors take it for the field of sharp edges; he adds that the numbers engaged were probably not large but the day a turning point.

Clarke suspects envy, Abner having often been out-generalled by David, canvasses four answers to the two years, that two years passed before any but Judah attached itself to David, that Abner effectively reigned the last five while his king kept the title, that Ishbosheth was forty when he had reigned two, or Houbigant's emendation of six for two, which he declines because every ancient version and every manuscript yet collated reads two; he calls the challenge diabolical play outright, gives the Targum's two renderings of the place-name, the portion of the mighty and the inheritance of those who were slain, and on the catching by the head recalls Alexander making the Macedonians shave because, as he told Parmenio, there is no better hold in battle than the beard. Wesley is blunter on Abner's motive, that he knew his king would have only the name while he kept the power, hears in the challenge a vain-glorious and cruel man and a soldier of fortune, and makes the place the field of rock, of men who stood unmovable, each dying where he fought.
Gill makes the kinship the hinge, Ner having been Saul's uncle and Abner his cousin.

18.pericope_label: And there were three sons of Zeruiah there, Joab, and Abishai, and Asahel: and Asahel was as light of foot as a wild roe. And Asahel pursued after Abner; and in going he turned not to the right hand nor to the left from following Abner. Then Abner looked behind him, and said, Art thou Asahel? And he answered, I am. And Abner said to him, Turn thee aside to thy right hand or to thy left, and lay thee hold on one of the young men, and take thee his armour. But Asahel would not turn aside from following of him. And Abner said again to Asahel, Turn thee aside from following me: wherefore should I smite thee to the ground? how then should I hold up my face to Joab thy brother? Howbeit he refused to turn aside: wherefore Abner with the hinder end of the spear smote him under the fifth rib, that the spear came out behind him; and he fell down there, and died in the same place: and it came to pass, that as many as came to the place where Asahel fell down and died stood still. Joab also and Abishai pursued after Abner: and the sun went down when they were come to the hill of Ammah, that lieth before Giah by the way of the wilderness of Gibeon.

schools.summary: Henry notes that Asahel got the name of being light of foot as a wild roe by swift pursuing and not swift flying, judges the design brave had he been equal to it, and closes with the tag that he perished in an attempt too vast for him; he draws the rule that in all contests it is wisdom to compare our own strength with our adversaries' and to take heed of being partial to ourselves in the comparison. On Abner's reluctance he goes further than the rest, suspecting that the care how he should lift up his face to Joab shows he really believed David would have the kingdom at last by the divine designation, and that in opposing him he was acting against his own conscience. He reads the blow as a back stroke with the hinder end of the spear, from which Asahel feared no danger, a pass he had not learned to guard against, observes that the fall put a full stop to the pursuit and gave Abner time to rally, and takes two lessons from it, that death often comes by ways we least suspect, since who would fear the butt end of a spear, and that we are betrayed by the accomplishments we are proud of.

Clarke supplies the ancient valuation of swiftness, reckoned a great accomplishment among the heroes, Homer giving Achilles the epithet of swift-footed no fewer than thirty times in the Ilias, and Roman soldiers being taught both to run swiftly and to swim well; he makes the chief cause of Abner's reluctance a fear of exciting Joab's enmity, until Asahel's obstinacy left the choice of killing or being killed, and reads the weapon differently from the others, taking the turning about to pierce him as what our version calls the hinder end, so that Abner ran the spear through with the point, and noting that the stroke cost Abner his own life in the next chapter. Wesley hears in the offer of a lesser antagonist an old and experienced captain telling the young man to try his skill on some raw soldier, and repeats Henry's second lesson almost word for word, that the swiftness Asahel presumed on forwarded his fate.

Keil and Delitzsch find that Abner did not want to put the young hero to death out of regard for Joab and their former friendship, say the lower end of the spear appears to have been pointed, put the wound in the abdomen with the spear coming out behind, and report that nothing further is known of the places named in the pursuit. Ellicott allows the extreme youth may have told but makes the chief cause a dread of Joab's vengeance, agrees the spears were sharpened at the hinder end for sticking into the ground, adds that the fifth rib, here and wherever else the phrase occurs, should be rendered abdomen, and conjectures from the way of the wilderness of Gibeon that the hill lay not far from that town, so the pursuit was not a long one.
Gill is less admiring of Asahel than the rest, having him trust his swiftness without considering that the race is not always to the swift, and that he was a raw young man matched against a veteran.

25.pericope_label: And the children of Benjamin gathered themselves together after Abner, and became one troop, and stood on the top of an hill. Then Abner called to Joab, and said, Shall the sword devour for ever? knowest thou not that it will be bitterness in the latter end? how long shall it be then, ere thou bid the people return from following their brethren? And Joab said, As God liveth, unless thou hadst spoken, surely then in the morning the people had gone up every one from following his brother. So Joab blew a trumpet, and all the people stood still, and pursued after Israel no more, neither fought they any more. And Abner and his men walked all that night through the plain, and passed over Jordan, and went through all Bithron, and they came to Mahanaim. And Joab returned from following Abner: and when he had gathered all the people together, there lacked of David’s servants nineteen men and Asahel. But the servants of David had smitten of Benjamin, and of Abner’s men, so that three hundred and threescore men died. And they took up Asahel, and buried him in the sepulchre of his father, which was in Beth–lehem. And Joab and his men went all night, and they came to Hebron at break of day.

schools.summary: Henry reads Abner's plea as self-interest confessing itself: the man most forward to fight was the first to have enough of it, and he who made a jest of bloodshed is shocked at it on the losing side, so that what was playing with the sword in the morning becomes the question whether the sword shall devour for ever, though it had devoured one day only and seemed long because it went against him. He draws two rules, that men use reason readily when it makes for them who would not use it if it made against them, and that the issue of things alters men's minds, since what looked pleasant in the morning looked dismal at night; and he adds that every sin is bitterness in the latter end, biting like a serpent those on whom it fawned. On Joab's reply he puts the aphorism that those forward to make mischief are commonly the first to complain of it, yet praises what followed, since Joab, pitying the mistake of his adversaries and scorning to make an army of Israelites pay for their commander's folly, stopped the pursuit by sound of trumpet, it being good husbandry to be sparing of blood. He closes with Wesley on the funeral.

Keil and Delitzsch take the plea at face value, a warning of the consequences of a desperate struggle and a call to end it, hold with Clarke and Wesley that Joab threw all the blame on the man who instigated the single combat, account for nineteen dead against three hundred and sixty by the quality of the troops, Joab's being the well-tried men who had gathered round David long before and Abner's the remnants of the army beaten upon Gilboa, and argue that Bithron must be a district and not a city since the text says all of it, rejecting both the old identification with Bethhoron in Aquila and the Vulgate and the modern conjecture of Bethharam. Ellicott wonders whether Abner was already weighing the expediency of transferring his allegiance to the house of David, having seen enough of Ishbosheth to know the tribes could never be united under him; he sets out the two constructions of Joab's answer and prefers the second, that Joab had meant to press the pursuit only until morning and was content to stop now, adds the advantage bow and spear give the pursuer, leaves it uncertain whether the figures include the twenty-four champions, and times the march home.

Clarke marks the day as the commencement of the civil wars and properly of the division of the two kingdoms, through which both nations were deluged with blood, and takes Joab's reply as throwing the blame on Abner for provoking the battle. Wesley takes it the same way, adding that all might have ended in an amicable agreement that morning had Abner so pleased, and closes with Henry on the funeral, that distinctions are made between the dust of some and of others but in the resurrection none will be made except between the godly and the ungodly.
